🐾 Here’s the story behind Matt’s payments work at **JP Morgan Chase**.

From **August 2009 to June 2012**, Matt served as Technology Delivery Lead for ACCESS Next Generation, the bank’s global corporate banking portal. Treasury operations ran across separate regional systems with different payment formats, client configurations, permissions, and compliance records. Bottomline Technologies’ WebSeries platform provided the foundation, but the bank needed custom engineering for its **135,000+ clients** across **180+ countries**. Corporate administrators spent days configuring permissions, while treasurers navigated separate regional payment systems.

Matt managed a blended team of **40+** **Accenture** and bank resources across the US, Mumbai, and Bangalore. He spent **70 to 80%** of his time embedded at Bottomline’s Portsmouth offices, working through where native platform capabilities ended and bank-specific development was required.

He designed and delivered payment modules for ACH credits and direct debits, wires, FX/cross-border payments, and federal tax payments. The work included NACHA file validation, embedded FX rate visibility, Message Authentication Code security, and payment-type-specific permissions. He also built contextual help explaining wire fields, tax codes, and cross-border requirements directly within payment workflows.

Alongside the payment engine, Matt designed the centralized gateway for message transformation, protocol translation, and routing across **12 countries**. He led payments data migration, preserving client configurations, entitlements, transaction histories, and compliance traceability without disrupting live payment operations. He also owned production incident response and coordinated root-cause analysis across the bank, offshore teams, and Bottomline.

For corporate administrators, his user administration engine replaced individual permission changes with bulk updates across users, accounts, and products. Entitlement management dropped from **days to minutes**, with a centralized dashboard showing who could access which payment functions.

ACCESS launched in **April 2011**. Corporate treasurers gained a single entry point for wire, ACH, and cross-border transfers across regional accounts, eliminating separate local logins, alongside real-time global reporting and single sign-on across treasury functions.

question: What's Matt's leadership philosophy?

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s how Matt describes his leadership philosophy.

Matt leads with empathy, clarity, and purpose. Most engineering teams he inherited were “over-processed, under-trusted, waiting for permission instead of owning outcomes.” His task was to create an environment where engineers, designers, and product teams could do the best work of their careers, with trust, clarity, and shared purpose rather than just process or tools.

He makes intent explicit, pushes decisions to the people closest to the work, and uses transparency, direct feedback, and open communication. He coaches teams to think clearly, not just execute tasks. He also grounds engineering culture in automation, continuous delivery, and quality-first practices, giving teams confidence in what they ship.

At the **Accenture** Cloud Innovation Center, teams had avoided risks because they feared blame. Matt introduced a “permit to fail” culture through non-punitive post-mortems and lean, low-stakes experiments. Teams discussed lessons rather than pointing fingers, applied those lessons to subsequent sprints, and began treating failed experiments as decision inputs rather than setbacks. Repeat errors declined and project timelines shortened.

He also built balanced teams of engineers, product managers, and UX architects with equal participation and shared accountability. Pair programming, collaborative coding, retrospectives, and knowledge-sharing sessions replaced role silos and reduced handoffs. Teams could voice feedback and implement changes autonomously.

At the Cloud Innovation Center, his leadership approach produced **4x delivery acceleration** once teams embraced lean product and modern engineering practices. The balanced-team work also reduced project delays, improved team satisfaction and retention, and achieved **zero-defect production code** across client engagements.

🐾 Here’s what Matt has built, delivered, and run.

Matt’s work centers on Execution & Delivery and Org & Working-Model Transformation: shipping enterprise platforms, changing how teams build software, and building the organization that delivers them.

At **Accenture**, clients were struggling with slow development cycles, siloed teams, and legacy systems. They needed more than a platform upgrade: they needed to move from waterfall and feature factories to iterative, customer-centric product development. Many new hires also lacked hands-on experience with cloud-native technologies or modern engineering practices.

Matt built the Atlanta and Tampa Cloud Innovation Centers from **0 to 150+ practitioners**, owning full P&L accountability, hiring, training, and career development. He brought product managers, designers, and engineers together in balanced teams, replacing functional handoffs with pair programming, test-driven development, and continuous delivery. He adapted those practices for enterprise security, compliance, and legacy-system constraints.

He also built the management machinery: pairing auditions, peer-driven feedback, promotion calibration, and compensation allocation. Junior hires worked with experienced mentors through an “I do, we do, you do” learning model. The organization achieved near-zero attrition in its first **2 years**.

The centers delivered **30+ product engagements** across **15+ Fortune 500 clients**, with **4X faster velocity** and **zero-defect deployments**. Delivery excellence and client relationships generated **\$100M+ in repeat business**.

His delivery work includes **JP Morgan Chase**, where he led a **40+ person** blended team and delivered a centralized payments gateway across **12 countries**, replacing fragmented regional integrations. At **RBC**, he established program governance, shared reporting, and explicit responsibilities across the bank, **Accenture**, and its technology partner.

Matt is seeking a role where building the product engineering organization, establishing the culture, and delivering results are part of the same job.

question: Why hire Matt?

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s a time Matt’s assumptions led to a production-data incident.

Matt was the tech lead on a global platform modernization delivery for a financial services client. The program was under delivery pressure, with offshore teams executing test cycles across development, QA, UAT, and production environments. IAM controls, environment segregation, and downstream access configurations had been inherited from prior phases, along with existing documentation.

Matt was responsible for ensuring a safe environment setup, but he relied on that documentation rather than verifying the controls. He focused on delivery pressures instead of validating access patterns. He did not audit who could trigger downstream jobs or email processes, implement compensating controls such as data masking and email interception, or verify whether production customer names and email addresses had been scrubbed from downstream environments.

An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT. It sent communications containing unmasked production customer data to **thousands of real clients**.

Matt took accountability and led the team through root cause analysis and remediation. They identified insufficient IAM checks, unclear environment boundaries, and production data that had not been scrubbed, then worked collectively to implement corrective controls.

The client demanded that the tester be removed from the project. Matt described this as “a systemic failure that resulted in an individual consequence.” His stated lesson was that “assumptions are risks in disguise.” IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership became day-one leadership responsibilities in his delivery approach.

At **Accenture’s** Liquid Studio, traditional training programs couldn’t keep pace with rapidly evolving AWS technologies. Gaps in cloud competency were slowing adoption, while engineers needed practical experience to lead cloud-native initiatives. Matt led AWS Launchpad at the Atlanta Innovation Hub from July **2018** to November **2019**, working with AWS to create a tailored enablement program.

He built the program around structured learning paths, hands-on labs, and mentor-based training rather than theory alone. The learning paths covered AWS core services and cloud-native application development, including Lambda, API Gateway, DynamoDB, Kubernetes, and ECS/Fargate. Certification preparation included AWS Solutions Architect and DevOps Engineer.

Matt delivered interactive workshops and labs that immersed engineers in real-world AWS environments. These sessions gave participants opportunities to apply what they were learning, rather than only study the services. He also established cloud expert mentorship teams to embed AWS best practices and build institutional knowledge beyond individual training sessions.

Group coaching sessions and knowledge-sharing workshops added ongoing support. Engineers could learn together, work with cloud experts, and continue developing their cloud competencies as technologies changed. The program’s scope was to build deep cloud competencies across **Accenture**, not just prepare a single project team for an exam.

More than **200 professionals earned AWS certifications** through the program. The program accelerated cloud adoption and the launch of cloud-native initiatives, with structured learning, practical application, and mentorship supporting continued capability-building across teams.
